transcript.text: I am the business intelligence analyst at a retailer that sells in its own shops and online across the UAE. The chief executive wants one weekly revenue dashboard, by region, channel and product category, that everyone trusts. Last month the sales director reported revenue about nine percent higher than finance did for the same weeks, and each says the other is wrong. Both teams start from the export I shared: one row per order with an order id, the order date, region, channel, product category, amount, status and customer id. The status column shows how each order ended. I would like the dashboard built from this table so I can present it at Monday's management meeting. The chief executive will use it to judge the regional managers. [shares sales.csv]

Two things already stand out. Let me size them.

I read your situation this way: you don't have a data-quality fight between sales and finance, you have an unagreed **definition of revenue**, and both teams are applying a different one to the same export. The dashboard is the deliverable, but the definition is the problem — and it matters more than usual here because the chief executive will read it as a report card on named people. What your table already shows:

- **The gap is the status column, almost exactly.** Across all 2,020 rows: paid 408,749.73, refunded 42,808.29, cancelled 21,330.31. For March 2026, counting refunded orders as revenue gives 24,688.08 against 22,456.18 if you count only paid — that is the "about nine percent" your sales director reported. Add cancellations and it becomes 26,122.16 versus 22,456.18. So neither of them is wrong; they are answering different questions, and one of those questions credits money that went back out of the building. - **Refunds are stored as positive amounts.** There is no negative amount anywhere in the table. So any sum of `amount` treats a refund as income unless the status is handled on purpose. - **2,020 rows, 2,000 distinct order ids.** A third, smaller disagreement waiting to happen for whoever counts rows. A manager in a high-refund region looks better under booked revenue than under net revenue, purely from how the column is treated. And since online orders carry a region too, part of what a regional manager is judged on is e-commerce they don't run. So I would not put a single contested number in front of the CEO without the definition written on it and the alternative visible beside it. My approach, and the plan:

1. **Reconcile** — prove where the gap sits, week by week, so Monday's meeting settles a definition instead of an argument. 2. **Fix the definition** in writing: net revenue (paid only) as the headline, refunds and cancellations as reported leakage rather than as a hidden subtraction. 3. **Clean once** — de-duplicate order ids, flag status, add an explicit net-revenue column. 4. **Build the weekly dashboard** on that table: region, channel, product category, with the definition stated in every tile. 5. **Stop condition:** the two teams' figures tie out to the dashboard for a named past week, within rounding, before it is used to assess anyone. The options above are those steps offered three ways. My advice is the first one: five minutes of reconciliation makes the dashboard something both directors will defend, whereas option two builds on sand unless you can already get the definition agreed by Monday. Whichever you pick, I'll run the cleaning preview before any rows come out.

transcript.text: I am the commercial director of a building-materials distributor. Last year we bought a competitor, so we now have two customer lists: about 4,000 accounts in our system and 2,500 in theirs. I want a customer lifetime value model on the combined list so we know which accounts deserve a key-account manager; we can afford one for about 150 accounts. Each system has its own account numbers. Company names were typed by hand, the same contractor often has a separate account for each building site or branch, and many firms bought from both of us. Both systems hold three years of invoices with the account number, date and amount. Nothing is exported yet. My sales reps say the big customers are obvious and the list should find the ones they miss.

Here's how I read it, and one thing I'd change about the brief.

**The problem.** You have a capacity decision: 150 key-account managers, and you want them on the customers whose value justifies it. A contractor with five site accounts can show up as five mid-sized rows: either they take five of your 150 slots, or they rank below the cut-off and you miss a genuinely large customer entirely. That is precisely the effect your reps are describing when they say the big ones are obvious — they know companies, your systems know accounts.

**What needs care before any work starts.**
- Three years of invoices with account number, date and amount gives you *revenue*, not *value*. In building materials, margin per euro varies enormously between commodity block and insulation, tiles or fixings. Ranking on revenue alone will systematically favour high-volume, thin-margin traders for your scarcest sales resource. If you cannot get cost or margin per line, we build a revenue CLV and say so on the list.
- Matching has to be a build step, not a model assumption. And a wrong merge is worse than no merge: two different firms with similar names (same surname, two brothers' businesses) would silently pool their revenue and both jump the cut-off. So the uncertain matches go to a human review queue.
- With three years only, a predicted-value model can be validated by holding back the most recent stretch and scoring against what actually happened. Anything beyond that is an assumption, not a measurement.

**The approach.** Resolve accounts to firms first, then put a value model on that. The obvious route — concatenate the two files and train on it — would produce a ranking that looks plausible and is wrong at the top, which is exactly where you spend money.

**The plan.** 1. Export both systems. 2. Build the firm master and check how many firms remain ambiguous. 3. Aggregate to firm level: revenue, recency, frequency, trend, site count. 4. Score and rank, then test the top-150 against your reps' existing key-account list and report how many they miss. 5. Refresh and re-validate on a schedule.

**The options above** cover where to start. I'd take the first: the customer master, because every later number depends on it — with the second as a quick diagnostic on the same export, if you want ammunition for the sales meeting. The third is the destination, not the first move.

To run any of it, export from each system: an account list (account number, legal and trading name, address with postcode, **tax/VAT registration number**, assigned rep, opening date) and the invoices (invoice number, account number, date, net and gross amount, product category, and unit cost or margin if you hold it).

One question that changes step 2 most: **do your account records carry a tax/VAT number, or a parent-company/group code?** If yes, matching is near-exact. If no, it rides on names and addresses and I'd budget real time for the review queue.

(I left out the parts whose numbers I cannot source from you or your data. Ask me about any part in words and I will go through it.)

choices.what: Once you export both account lists and both invoice files, DCLab matches accounts to one real customer per firm - exact on tax/VAT number where you have it, then fuzzy on name plus address/postcode, then a review list of the uncertain pairs for a human to settle. Every account keeps its history, rolled up under one firm. You get: One table where a contractor with four site accounts is one customer with four billing accounts - the unit your 150 key-account slots should be counted against. Trade-off: No lifetime-value ranking on day one. And a wrong merge is worse than no merge, so the fuzzy part keeps a review queue rather than deciding silently. Effort: Half a day of exporting; the matching pass itself is quick. Do it before any model.

You get: A hard number for the sales meeting on how much the two-list split distorts the 'obvious' big customers, plus the real scale of the matching job. Trade-off: This is the right destination but the wrong first move - trained on accounts rather than firms it would hand one contractor several of your 150 slots and leak duplicates into the validation. Effort: Longest step; needs the master from option 1 as its input.

Started: the customer master. Nothing runs until the files are in, so here is exactly what happens and in what order.

**What to send me** — four files, two per system, CSV or Excel, all accounts not just active ones:
- *Account master:* account number, legal name, trading name, address with postcode, tax/VAT number, assigned rep, account opening date.
- *Invoices:* invoice number, account number, date, net and gross amount, product category, and unit cost or margin if the system holds it.

**Then the build, in order.**
1. Normalise names and addresses across both systems (J & Sons Ltd vs J&Sons Limited vs trading-as names, postcode spacing).
2. Match in tiers, strictest first: tax/VAT number is a near-exact join; then normalised name plus postcode; then a fuzzy name-and-address comparison. Anything uncertain does not get merged automatically — it goes into a review queue with both candidate accounts, their revenue and their rep, so a person decides.
3. Collapse site and branch accounts under one firm ID, while keeping each original account number. That matters for the later model: value is measured per firm, but you can still see how many sites a firm runs, which is itself a signal.
4. A wrong merge there is the only mistake that costs you a key-account manager.
5. Deliver the master: one row per firm, both systems' account numbers, region, and three years of revenue at firm level, ready to feed the lifetime-value ranking.

When you send the files, tell me in one line whether the tax/VAT column actually comes out of both systems. If it doesn't, I'll plan for a bigger review queue and a stricter hand-check at the top, rather than promise a clean automatic merge.
